children: India produced 247.87 million tonne of milk in 2024–25, nearly a quarter of global output. Yet an equally important question is how much value survives the journey from farm to consumer.

Milk is perishable, and dairy wastage is not limited to products visibly spoiling. It includes shelf life lost through temperature fluctuations, inventory ageing in warehouses and dark stores, forced discounting near expiry, avoidable returns and cash locked in the wrong stock. By the time a product is discarded, the industry has already spent on procurement, processing, packaging, energy and transportation.
The hidden cost of wastage is, therefore, not simply operational. It weakens the economics of the entire dairy value chain.
The cold chain is the first line of defence

A robust cold chain begins with prompt chilling after milk collection and continues through processing, storage, transportation, distribution and retail. A break at any point can compromise quality and shorten the effective selling window, even if the product has not visibly deteriorated.

This makes temperature control a shared responsibility, not something that ends at the dairy factory gate. The latest FSSAI advisory reinforces the need for appropriate temperature-controlled handling, storage and transportation of perishable foods, including paneer and khoa. Compliance is essential for food safety; consistent execution also protects freshness, reduces losses and safeguards consumer trust.

As organised retail and quick commerce expand, the weakest link can increasingly be the last mile: a distributor’s cold room, a dark store or the journey to the consumer. We need end-to-end temperature discipline, monitoring and accountability across every handoff.
Inventory must follow demand, not the other way around
Better refrigeration alone will not solve wastage. Dairy businesses also need sharper demand forecasting and more agile inventory management.

Milk moves fresh and daily; it cannot be planned like long-shelf-life packaged goods. Value-added products, meanwhile, differ widely in shelf life and demand patterns. Curd, paneer and yogurt need frequent replenishment, while ghee, butter and milk powder can also help balance seasonal milk availability.
The objective is not simply to minimise inventory. It is to hold the right inventory, in the right location, for the right duration.

That requires integrating store-level sales data, seasonal patterns, festivals and weather with milk procurement, production and distribution plans. Batch-level visibility and first-expiry-first-out rotation must extend beyond factories to distributors, modern trade and quick-commerce platforms.

For value-added dairy products, our planning principle should be to deliver at least 75 per cent of the declared shelf life remaining, wherever operationally applicable. This is a more meaningful freshness objective than allowing products to approach expiry before they reach the consumer.

Flexible manufacturing adds another safeguard. The ability to balance milk between liquid products, cultured dairy, fat products and powders, within technological and market constraints, helps manage seasonal surpluses without distress selling or unnecessary inventory build-up.
But the real opportunity lies in connecting three capabilities: an unbroken cold chain, accurate demand sensing and disciplined inventory rotation. Each reinforces the other.

Reducing wastage frees up capital, protects product quality and improves the economic value realised from every litre procured. It creates more room to invest in farmer linkages, innovation and affordability.
India has proved that it can produce milk at scale. The next measure of progress should be how much of that milk’s value we preserve, right up to the consumer.
The author is CEO, Heritage Foods Ltd.

title: The hidden cost of wastage: Rethinking inventory management in India’s dairy industry
